translation: Two other small, scallop-edged photos, probably from the same year, show the same child, but more tiny in a dress with flounces and balloon sleeves.
In the first one, she nestles impishly against a bulky woman encased in a wide-striped dress with her hair rolled up high.
In the other one, she lifts her left fist while her right is held by a tall man in light colored jacket and pleated trousers who is standing somewhat nonchalantly.
Both photos were taken on the same day in front of a short wall topped by flower beds situated within a paved courtyard.
Above their heads goes a clothesline where one clothespin still remains hanging.

Another photo, signed by the same photographer but on more ordinary paper and without the gold border probably intended for the same distribution among family members shows a little girl of around four years old, serious, almost sad despite a chubby, cheery face under her short hair, parted in the middle and pulled back with clips to which ribbons are attached like butterflies.
Her left hand rests on the same carved Louis XVI style table, entirely visible this time.
She seems pudgy in her pinafore dress that is hiked up at the front due to a protruding belly maybe a sign of rickets (around 1944).
The boys were proud to join the regiment, and everyone thought they looked grand in their uniforms.
On the evening of their enlistment, they did rounds in the cafes to celebrate their acknowledgement as real men.
Before joining the army, they were still children who had little worth on the job market or in marriage.
Afterward, they would be able to have a wife and children.
The uniform which they would flaunt around their neighborhood during leave enveloped them with patriotic beauty and potential sacrifice.
The shadow of victorious warriors—of GIs—loomed around them.
The coarse woolen fabric of their jackets grazed when you went on tiptoe to kiss them signified the absolute divide between men's world and women's world.
Seeing them roused feelings of heroism.

Amid the unchanging, last year's circus posters with Roger Lanzac's photo, first communion pictures given to friends, the Club des Chansonniers on Luxembourg Radio, filled their days with new desires.
On Sunday afternoons, crowds gathered in front of the shop window of the general electricity store to watch television.
Cafes invested in buying a set to attract customers.
Motocross tracks snaked up and down hillsides, with people watching deafening vehicles ascend and descend all day long.
The growing impatience of commerce shaking up life's routine in towns with its new slogans: 'initiative', 'dynamism'.
Between fairgrounds and festivals, fortnightly sales became a springtime ritual.
In city centres loudspeakers bellowed invitations to buy intermixed with songs by Annie Cordy and Eddie Constantine all for a chance at winning either a Simca car or dining room furniture.

On stage at Mayor's Square , a local entertainer would tell jokes from Roger Nicolas' or Jean Richard's repertoire; he called up contestants for Singing Contests or Double or Quits games just like on radio shows; ensconced in one corner of the stage sat under her crown was Queen Commerce .
Merchandise advanced under festive flags .
People expressed sentiments such as "Things are changing" or "We mustn't get stuck in our waysstaying at home dulls your mind".
But they only talked about what they had seen, which could be relived by eating and drinking.
They did not have enough talent or conviction to talk about what they knew but had not seen.
So neither of Jewish children boarding trains for Auschwitz, nor of the starving people picked up in the morning in the Warsaw Ghetto, nor of the 10,000 degrees at Hiroshima.

Hence this impression that history classes, documentaries and films later would not dispel: neither the crematory ovens nor the atomic bomb were in the same era as black market butter, air raid warnings and trips to the basement.
They shifted gears by comparison to the war before, the Great War, that of '14, won, marked by both blood and glory.
It was a war of men which the women at the table listened to with reverence.
They spoke of Chemin des Dames and Verdun, of gas attack victims and the toll of bells on November 11th 1918.
They named villages from which not a single child who had gone to the front returned.
They compared soldiers in trench mud to prisoners in '40, warm and secure for five years without even experiencing bombs falling overhead.
Heroism and sorrow were their points of contention.

The children were not listening and were quick to leave the table as soon as they had permission, taking advantage of the general goodwill on festive days to engage in forbidden games, bouncing on the beds and swinging upside down.
But they absorbed everything.

Next to the fabulous time of which they would not arrange episodes for a long while the Debacle, The Exodus, The Occupation, The Landing, The Victory seemed duller than their unnamed era where they just grew up.
They wished they had been born or at least been older when there was a requirement to travel en masse along roads and sleep on straw like gypsies.
From this unlived period they would keep persistent regret.
Recollecting others' experiences gave them a secret nostalgia for that time period that narrowly missed them out but also an anticipation of experiencing it someday.
The frenzy that had followed the Liberation was fading.
People only thought about going out and the world was full of desires to be satisfied immediately.
Everything that constituted a first time since the war sparked a rush: bananas, National Lottery tickets, fireworks.

Whole neighborhoods, from grandmothers supported by their daughters to infants in strollers, threw themselves at the fair, torchlight retreats, Bouglione Circus where they risked being trampled in the scramble.
They gathered like praying and singing crowds on the road to welcome back Our Lady of Boulogne's statue and escort her for miles on end the following day.
Secular or religious, any occasion served as a good reason for them to be outside together as though they wanted to continue living collectively.

On Sunday evenings busloads wouldn't return from sea without rowdy young men in shorts belting songs atop roof racks attached with luggage; dogs roamed freely and were mating right there in broad daylight street.
Family narratives and social narratives are intertwined.

The voices of the guests carved out the spaces of their youth: the countryside and farms where, from lost memory, men had been clerks and girls had been maids; the factory where they all met, milled about, and got married; the small businesses that were opened by those with bigger ambitions.
These voices were portraying stories with no personal events apart from births, weddings, and farewells.
Lives filled with work, its harshness and weariness as well as threats from drink.
School served as a mythical background a brief golden age dominated by a strict teacher god armed with an iron ruler for slapping their fingers.
Brown pictures passed from hand to hand, their backs stained by every finger that had held them during other meals—a mix of coffee and grease melded into an indescribable colour.
In the stiff and solemn couples, the wedding guests lined up on several rows along a wall, one didn't recognise either their parents or anyone else.
It was not oneself either that was seen in the half-naked baby of indistinct gender lying on a cushion but someone else—a creature belonging to a mute and inaccessible time.
